e.t: This noun means “ignorance”—a lack of knowledge or understanding. It names a condition in which someone does not know or recognize what is true. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including passages in Job, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense remains the absence of knowledge or understanding.

This verb means to injure someone or treat someone unjustly. It describes wrongdoing that harms another person or acts unfairly toward them, rather than merely naming a private feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish books represented here, it occurs 79 times, so it can describe unjust treatment in a range of settings. Its central sense remains active: someone causes harm or deals wrongly with another. The wording “injure; unjust to” captures both the harmful action and its unjust character.

Azer is a proper name, preserved as “Azer” in the Greek Old Testament translation. It functions as a personal name rather than as a common word describing an action, object, or quality. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 12:10. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role or the name’s significance in that passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to someone identified as Ailous or Elus. It is not a common noun describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation within the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:13 and 33:14. Without the surrounding verse text, no further personal details or contextual significance can be stated from the name alone.

This adjective means “exact” or “accurate.” It describes something that corresponds closely to what is true, correct, or intended, without imprecision. It can characterize a statement, understanding, measurement, or description that is dependable in its details. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, this word occurs eight times: four times in Old Testament books and four times in deuterocanonical writings. Its references range from Esther and Daniel to Sirach, showing ordinary use for precision and correctness rather than a specialized religious term.

“Fisherman” refers to a person who catches fish. It is a noun naming someone whose work or activity is fishing, rather than the fish, the net, or the place where fishing occurs. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, the word appears four times, in four separate verses. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a human fisherman. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is part of a literal description or a larger picture, but the word itself identifies the person engaged in catching fish.

“Otherwise” is an adverb that points to a different way, condition, or result than the one being discussed. It can redirect the reader from one possibility to another, showing that something would be understood or happen differently under another circumstance. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs 10 times across 9 verses, in Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any verse depends on the sentence around it.

This noun means “vine,” referring to a plant that bears grapes. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for literal vines in descriptions of plants, land, harvest, and household blessing. It occurs 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX material, showing a recurring agricultural image throughout these writings. The word may appear in singular or plural translation, but its basic meaning remains the same: a grape-bearing plant. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective means “lawless,” describing a person or thing marked by disregard for rightful law. It identifies conduct or character as opposed to what is lawful, rather than naming a particular action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 82 times, showing that it is used repeatedly for people or behavior associated with lawlessness. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Antilibanos” or “Antilivanos.” It identifies a named place or geographical feature in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or person in general. The word occurs five times, in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its precise referent in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to name a specific location.

This verb means “demand back”: to require something to be returned or repaid. It describes an active claim made against someone who holds what is owed, rather than a passive request. In the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom text, it occurs nine times, so its central idea remains consistent across several settings. The surrounding verse determines whether what is demanded back is a debt, possession, or obligation.

This verb means to refute thoroughly—to answer a claim by exposing it as wrong or unable to stand. It describes a strong, complete rebuttal rather than a brief disagreement. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and argument, but its central idea is a decisive refutation.

The verb means “attribute”: it describes assigning something to a person or source, crediting it to them rather than merely mentioning it. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone attributes something to someone or something else. This LXX word occurs three times in its corpus, appearing once in Deuteronomy and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead astray”: it describes causing someone to move away from the proper path or direction. It is an action word, focusing on the one who misdirects another rather than merely describing a person who is lost. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring use for misleading or turning someone away. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek Old Testament adjective means “of juniper; of cedar.” It identifies something as belonging to, associated with, or made from juniper or cedar. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in three verses across 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its precise reference in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its normal function is to describe a material or feature connected with one of these trees.

Artaxerxes is a proper name for a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the Persian ruler named Artaxerxes, rather than describing a quality, action, or general object. The name appears 24 times in the Greek Old Testament, chiefly in Esther and once in Daniel. Its first listed occurrence is Esther 1:1, and its last is Daniel 6:1. Because it is a personal name, the surrounding passage is needed to understand what this ruler is doing or how he relates to the events described.

This adjective describes someone or something as “urbane”—polished, cultivated, and socially refined. It points to a manner that is pleasant, well-mannered, or suited to respectable society rather than rough or unpolished. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus. Its exact force in any verse depends on the person or thing it describes and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “incorruptibility; integrity.” It names a quality of being uncorrupted and whole, describing what remains sound rather than spoiled, damaged, or compromised. As a noun, it refers to this quality itself, whether viewed as freedom from corruption or as complete moral and personal soundness. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains lasting incorruptibility and integrity.

Balanas, also rendered Valanas, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:28. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role in that passage cannot be explained further; the lexical information establishes the name itself and its alternate rendering.

Bamōth, also rendered Vamoth, is a proper name for a place. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a separate action or quality; its role is to identify a location in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Numbers 21:19–20. The precise significance of the place in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense supplied for the name is simply Bamōth or Vamoth.

This adjective means “regal” or “royal,” describing something connected with a king, royal authority, or the royal court. It can characterize people, places, possessions, actions, or settings associated with kingship. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 33 times across 31 verses, showing a recurring description of what belongs to or reflects royal status. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “scream,” referring to a loud vocal outcry. As a noun, it names the sound itself rather than an action someone performs. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 14 times, so it is used across more than one setting while retaining this basic sense. The surrounding verse determines whose scream is meant and what prompted it; the word itself identifies the vocal outcry.

Ganathōn is a proper name rendered as “Ganathōn” or “Ganathon.” It functions as a personal or other identifying name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 10:7 and Nehemiah 12:16. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supports identification, but does not establish additional meaning or significance.

This word is a proper name, identifying a named person or entity rather than describing an action or quality. It is given as “Gēbi” and “Yivi,” preserving the name in the Greek LXX text. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 11:8. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its precise identity in that passage cannot be stated beyond its function as a personal or proper name.

This adjective means “shaggy,” describing a person, animal, or other thing with a rough, thick, or untrimmed covering of hair. It identifies outward appearance rather than an action or inner quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 10 times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and 2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a noticeably hairy or rough appearance.

Debēlaim is a proper name, referring to a specific person, place, or thing identified by the surrounding passage rather than describing a general idea or action. It is rendered “Debēlaim” and is also associated with the form “Thevilem.” In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in Hosea 1:3. Because the verse text and wider context are not included here, its precise identity cannot be determined from the name alone.

This noun refers to a bond or a condition of confinement—being restrained, held, or kept from freedom. It can describe physical bonds used to secure someone or something, and more broadly the state of imprisonment or restriction. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 44 times, showing repeated use for restraint and confinement rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “step,” referring to a person’s movement or the steps someone takes. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 16 times across 15 verses, especially in the Psalms, and is also found in 2 Samuel, Job, Proverbs, and Song of Songs. The word can describe ordinary physical movement, while its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence. Its basic sense remains a step or movement made while walking.

This LXX verb means “break apart.” It describes separating something into pieces or causing it to come apart, rather than merely moving or changing it. As a verb, it expresses an action performed or undergone. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Leviticus, Isaiah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being broken apart and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “leap about.” It describes a person or thing moving through lively, active jumps rather than simply standing or walking. Its central idea is bounding movement from place to place. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:9, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context. At the word level, it expresses the action of leaping about, whether understood as a single burst of movement or continued jumping.

This noun means “breach” or “gap”: an opening where something has been broken, divided, or left incomplete. It names the break itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 4:1. The word therefore points to a physical or structural opening in that passage, while the surrounding verse determines its particular force. Its central idea remains an interruption in a barrier or a missing section that leaves an opening.

This adjective means “diaphanous”: describing something sheer, delicate, or transparent enough to let light pass through. It refers to the quality of a material or object rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Esther, and Isaiah. Its exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains something light, thin, or see-through.

This noun means “rightness” or “right standing.” It describes a condition of being rightly aligned with what is good and just. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly, appearing 294 times, so its exact emphasis may depend on the surrounding sentence. The word can describe the quality or status of what is right rather than an action itself. Its earliest recorded use is in Genesis 15:6, and it continues through the later Greek biblical writings.

This noun means an “undertaking” or an “attempt”: something a person sets out to do or tries to accomplish. It names an effort considered as a thing in itself, rather than describing the person who performs it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah, at Jeremiah 23:20 and Jeremiah 37:24. Those references identify where the word occurs, while its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes a multitude of people—a large gathered body rather than a single person. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying something associated with or characterized by many people. Its recorded use is limited to one occurrence in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in 4 Maccabees 7:11. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but the word’s basic sense is a numerous human gathering.

This word means “centurion,” a noun naming a military officer. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 2 Kings 11:10 and 2 Kings 11:15. Its basic function is to identify a person by this official title rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. Because no verse text is included here, the precise role of the centurion in either passage must be understood from the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “wash out.” It describes the act of rinsing or cleansing something so that its contents or residue are removed. The word is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 6:21. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding instructions, but its basic meaning remains the action of washing something out. This verb means “pour out” or describes something being “drained.” It expresses the act of emptying a liquid or substance from one place or container into another, or of letting it flow away. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 133 times, so it describes a broad and repeated action rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being poured out and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “receive less,” describing getting a smaller amount than something else or than expected. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 14:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains an expression of reduced receiving or lesser portion, rather than a broad term for receiving in general.

Elia is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in Ezra. The name is preserved as “Elia,” and the available lexical information does not provide an additional ordinary meaning beyond this name. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Emmer, also rendered Emmir, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person by name. It occurs eight times across eight verses, appearing in passages from 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Jeremiah. Its significance in any particular passage depends on which named person is being mentioned there; the name itself does not carry an additional descriptive meaning in the available lexical definition.

gl: with the breath in one; breathing
d: with the breath in one; breathing

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something with breath in it—living, breathing rather than lifeless. It can point to the presence of breath itself, so its central idea is being alive in a physical sense. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the basic meaning remains “with the breath in one; breathing.”

This verb means “know accurately”: to possess clear, precise knowledge rather than a vague or mistaken understanding. It describes the act of recognizing or understanding something correctly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Numbers 23:10, Job 28:3, and Daniel 7:19. The surrounding verse determines what is being known, but the word itself emphasizes accuracy and certainty in knowing.

This Greek LXX verb means “empty themselves.” It describes an action in which the subjects themselves are emptied or pour out what they contain, rather than merely being acted upon from outside. The wording is reflexive: the action turns back upon those performing it. It occurs five times in the LXX corpus, four times in Psalms and once in Wisdom, so its basic sense is consistent across these passages, while the surrounding verse determines what is being emptied.

This Greek LXX verb means to “mount” or “step on.” It describes moving onto something or getting onto a person, animal, or elevated place. The word can therefore refer to mounting a ride or stepping onto a surface, while the surrounding sentence determines the specific object involved. It occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a repeated action word rather than a title or abstract idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “prevail”: to become stronger, gain the upper hand, or overcome opposing circumstances. It describes a person, force, or condition that succeeds in exerting control or proving stronger than what resists it. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across various situations rather than being limited to one setting.

This noun means “care”: thoughtful attention given to a person, matter, or need. It describes concern expressed through attentiveness and responsible concern rather than mere passing interest. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs nine times, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding passage determines whether the care is directed toward people, bodily well-being, wisdom, or a practical task. The word appears especially in Proverbs, where care is connected with what benefits and preserves life. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “set a mark upon.” It describes placing a mark on something or someone, identifying or indicating it in some way. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here: once in Job and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of marking or designating something. The supplied lexical definition supports this basic meaning directly.

This word means a hearth or fireplace—the place where fire is kept or used. It is a noun for a physical structure or surface associated with fire, including the hearth connected with worship furnishings and preparing offerings. In the Septuagint corpus, it occurs 14 times, chiefly in Old Testament passages and once in Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description of the object or activity involving the fire.

This adjective describes something that is cheap or easily paid for. It refers to low cost rather than great expense, and normally characterizes an object or possession. In the Greek LXX, it occurs four times, all in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains something obtainable for little payment.

This Greek LXX noun means “hero,” referring to a person regarded as unusually brave, strong, or distinguished. It is a title or description for such a person rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 46:28–29. The exact force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a heroic or celebrated person.

Thamni is a proper name, referring to someone identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times across three verses, in Judges and 1 Kings. The name is rendered “Thamni,” preserving it rather than translating it as a descriptive word. By itself, Thamni identifies a person but does not state that person’s character, role, or actions; those details must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

Thethēr, also rendered Thethir, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Joshua 15:59. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name’s precise location and role must be understood from that passage itself.

Idia, also rendered Ithia, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its ordinary lexical sense is simply the personal name itself. This name occurs 19 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. The available information does not establish a further meaning or etymology for the name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iebousaios” or “Ievuseos.” It identifies a named people or group in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It occurs 36 times across 34 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Zechariah. Because the available information gives the name but not the wording of those verses, its specific reference in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “sit” or “settle.” It describes taking a seated position or remaining settled in a place. The word is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament, with 178 occurrences, so its exact force can range from simply sitting to staying or dwelling, depending on the sentence. It is a straightforward action word rather than a title or abstract quality. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the ashes left from a burnt sacrifice. It names the material residue of something consumed by fire, rather than the offering itself or the act of burning. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Leviticus 6:3–4. Its precise use in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains specific: ashes associated with a burnt sacrifice.

“Wear down” is a verb describing the act of making someone or something weaker, more exhausted, or less able to continue. It focuses on the effect of continued pressure, difficulty, or exertion rather than on a single moment. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, at 2:2 and 2:13. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Kisaias, also rendered Kiseas, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in three verses across 1 Chronicles and Esther. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the person designated by this name.

gl: part between the knee and ankle; leg
d: part between the knee and ankle; leg

e.t: This noun means the part of the body between the knee and ankle—the lower leg. It refers to a physical body part and may be rendered simply as “leg” when describing a person’s limbs. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs five times, appearing in Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalms, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “livestock” or “animal,” referring generally to a living creature kept, counted, or discussed as property. It is a broad word rather than the name of one particular species. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs 246 times, showing regular use in descriptions of created creatures, household or owned animals, and animals included in ordinary laws and accounts. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Lais, also rendered Les, is a proper name—a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 25:44. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself identifies a person or named figure, while the passage supplies the details about whom it refers to. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name “Lais” or “Les,” not an abstract idea or general description.

This word means to account for something or count it—that is, to assess, reckon, or regard it in a particular way. As a verb, it describes the act of treating something as having a certain value or standing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 110 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through the later writings, so it serves a broad purpose in describing how people or God evaluate, calculate, or regard matters. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

In the Greek Old Testament, this word means “finally” or “remainder.” As an adjective, it can point to what is left over—the remaining portion—or mark what comes at the end. Its 72 occurrences across the LXX corpus show that it serves both a descriptive sense about what remains and an ordering sense about what follows last. The surrounding wording determines which sense is intended in a particular verse.

Makchi, also rendered Makkhi, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek LXX text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Numbers 13:15. The available lexical information establishes the name and its identity, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in that passage.

This adjective describes something as “like madness” or “mad.” It points to behavior, speech, or a condition that appears irrational or out of control, rather than calm and sensible. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 5:45. That single occurrence establishes its basic descriptive function, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what person or action it describes there. Its central idea remains the appearance or reality of madness.

Maserephōthmaim, also rendered Maserefothmem, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 13:6. Since the available record identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text or a further definition, its basic meaning is the name itself; its precise referent is established by the context of Joshua 13:6.

This Greek LXX verb means “blacken” or “become black.” It describes a change in color toward blackness, whether something is made dark or grows dark. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Song of Songs and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the darkening or blackening of something.

“Mērōz” or “Miroz” is a proper name, rendered as Meroz in Judges 5:23. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs only once, at Judges 5:23. The name itself does not provide a broader lexical definition; understanding its particular reference requires the verse and its surrounding passage.

Moni is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 18:24, and is rendered “Moni.” Because the supplied material does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it does not establish more about whom or what Moni identifies. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context of Joshua 18:24.

Nachoth is a proper name, rendered as “Nachoth” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but as the identifying name itself. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Genesis 36:13 and Genesis 36:17. The available lexical definition gives “Nachoth; Nakhoth,” preserving the name rather than translating it into an ordinary English meaning.

The word means “lawfully.” As an adverb, it describes how an action is performed—according to law or in a lawful manner. Its basic focus is not the person acting but the character of the action: the action conforms to law. Within this LXX usage, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 6:18; the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific force there.

Odouia, also rendered Othoia, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Chronicles 3:24 and once in Nehemiah 10:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the person’s family, role, or historical importance; those details belong to the passages where it appears.

This Greek LXX noun means “desire”—an inward longing or strong wish for something. It describes what a person wants or yearns for, whether that desire is directed rightly or needs restraint. The word occurs eight times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings, including Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is desired and how the surrounding sentence presents that desire.

This noun refers to a stronghold—a fortified place associated with protection, defense, or security. It can describe a physical defensive location rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 66 times, showing that this is an established term for a place of strength or refuge. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject.

This adjective describes something as “all-mingled; promiscuous”—mixed together without clear separation or distinction. It can describe a condition in which different people or things are gathered into one mixture rather than kept apart. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is complete or indiscriminate mingling.

This Greek verb means to urge someone forward or stimulate them to action. It describes active encouragement that moves a person toward doing something, rather than merely expressing approval or giving information. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 15:17 and 4 Maccabees 12:6. Since the surrounding verse text is not included, those references establish where it appears but do not determine the specific nuance in either passage.

This verb means “build round”: to construct something around or encircle it with building. It describes an act of surrounding a place or object with a built structure, rather than simply making something in general. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Job, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being surrounded and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains construction that forms an enclosing boundary.

This adjective means “embroidered,” describing something decorated by stitching or ornamental needlework. It is a descriptive word rather than the name of an object, so its exact force depends on the noun it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 35:35. The word therefore points to crafted, patterned decoration, while the surrounding passage determines what particular embroidered item is being described.

gl: maintain war with; keep up war
d: maintain war with; keep up war

e.t: This verb means “maintain war with” or “keep up war.” It describes continuing or sustaining a conflict rather than merely beginning one. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees, where its subject is presented as persisting in warfare. The word therefore focuses on the ongoing character of military conflict. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being described.

This LXX verb means “dispatch ahead” or “send forth.” It describes sending someone or something onward, often with the idea of going before or being sent out for a purpose. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or quality. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is sending forth or arranging for someone to go ahead.

This noun refers to “besieging” or “assiduity”—persistent, sustained attention or effort.
